t: The most formal dress code there is.
d: White tie is reserved for state dinners, royal events and some galas and balls. Men wear a black tailcoat, white piqué waistcoat and bow tie; women wear floor-length evening gowns, often with long gloves.
o: Evolved from 19th-century formal evening dress in Europe and remains the top of the Western dress-code ladder.
k: Black tailcoat and trousers with braid
White piqué waistcoat and bow tie
do: Hire from a specialist if you rarely attend
st: Confirm the invitation truly says white tie
w: Guests at state, royal or the most formal charity events.
b: Hiring is far cheaper than buying for one-off events.

d: Black tie means a dinner jacket (tuxedo) with a black bow tie for men, and a floor-length gown or very elegant cocktail-length dress for women. 'Black tie optional' allows a dark suit instead.
o: The dinner jacket appeared in the 1860s–1880s as a less formal alternative to the tailcoat.
k: Black or midnight dinner jacket with satin lapels
White dress shirt and black bow tie
do: Tie a real bow tie if you can
dont: Wear a business suit to strict black tie
Choose casual fabrics like cotton jersey
st: Check if it's 'black tie' or 'black tie optional'
Get a tuxedo fitted or hired
b: A well-fitted owned tuxedo pays off after about three hires.

d: Cocktail attire sits between black tie and business: suits (ties optional at many events) for men, and knee-to-midi dresses, dressy jumpsuits or elegant separates for women. It allows more colour and personality.
o: Grew out of 1920s cocktail parties and became a standard dress code mid-century.
k: Dark suit with or without tie
do: Match formality to the venue and time
dont: Go floor-length unless the event leans formal
st: Pick a dark suit or knee-length dress
b: Rent a statement dress or style a suit you already own.

t: Suits, ties and the most conservative workwear.
d: Business formal means a dark, matching suit with a dress shirt and tie, or a tailored suit, sheath dress or skirt suit with closed shoes. It's for interviews, boardrooms, court and formal client meetings.
o: Codified by 20th-century corporate and legal dress norms.
dont: Wear open-toe shoes in very formal settings
st: Buy one navy or charcoal suit
Add two shirts and one tie
w: Interviews, finance, law and senior client meetings.
b: A navy suit worn as separates doubles its value.

t: Relaxed, but clearly made an effort.
d: Smart casual pairs relaxed items with sharper ones: chinos or dark jeans with a blazer or knit, a blouse with tailored trousers, clean leather sneakers or loafers. It's the most common (and most confusing) dress code.
o: Emerged in the late 20th century as workplaces and social events relaxed formal codes.
do: Pair one smart piece with one casual piece
dont: Wear gym wear or ripped jeans
Overdress in a full suit and tie
st: Finish with loafers or clean leather sneakers
w: Dinners, dates, creative offices and many events.
b: Most of the look is pieces you already own; add one blazer.

t: Cocktail attire with sparkle, colour and seasonal fun.
d: Festive attire invites guests to bring colour, sequins, velvet and playful accessories to holiday and celebration events, usually at cocktail level of formality.
o: A modern invitation wording that grew popular in the 2000s for holiday parties and New Year's events.
do: Add one sparkly or seasonal element
dont: Wear novelty jumpers unless invited to
Go head-to-toe sequins at a dinner
b: Rent sequins once; buy velvet you can rewear.

t: Free-spirited weddings: pampas, macramé and golden hour.
d: A boho wedding favours relaxed outdoor settings, flowing dresses, dried and wild flowers, macramé, rugs and lanterns, with an earthy palette and a laid-back timeline.
o: Popularised in the 2010s by festival culture and destination weddings.
do: Choose an outdoor or natural venue
st: Plan one macramé or floral focal point
w: Couples who want a relaxed, nature-loving celebration.
b: Dried flowers can be bought in bulk and reused for decor.

t: Timeless ballroom romance: white florals, candlelight and black tie.
d: A classic elegant wedding uses a formal venue, white and green florals, candlelight, fine linens and a structured timeline, often with a black-tie dress code.
o: Built on traditional Western wedding conventions that have changed little in a century.
st: Specify black tie or formal attire
w: Couples who love tradition and formality.
b: Candles and greenery give elegance for less than all-white floral walls.

t: Country charm: wood, string lights and wildflowers.
d: A rustic barn wedding is set in a barn or farm, decorated with wood, burlap or linen, string lights, wildflowers and family-style dining. It feels warm and community-focused.
o: Grew popular in North America in the 2000s–2010s as couples sought relaxed, personal venues.
st: Book a barn with good facilities
w: Country lovers and couples hosting family-centred celebrations.
b: Local wildflowers and DIY jars keep costs low.

t: Clean lines, gallery venues and statement simplicity.
d: A modern minimalist wedding uses architectural venues, a restrained palette, sculptural florals, clean typography and sleek attire. Every detail is intentional.
o: Reflects the influence of minimalist design and editorial weddings from the 2010s onward.
dont: Make it feel cold: warm the lighting
w: Design-minded couples who love clean aesthetics.
b: Fewer, bigger statements often cost less than many small decorations.
